extracted.intended_audience: physicians, surgeons, natural philosophers, and Royal Society readers (early modern experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting observational and interventional experiments in medicine and natural history (animal trials, human case trials, procedural description, and demonstration of effects). Emphasis on reproducible procedure, witness verification, and comparison to usual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal experimentation prior to human trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform experiments on brutes (animals) repeatedly and observe consistent success before trying the remedy on men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states that experiments on animals 'having so well succeeded on brutes, and been repeated over and over with the like success, no scruple was then made to try the liquor upon men.' Use multiple animal trials as a prerequisite for human application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed procedural description of application
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe precisely how the treatment is applied (e.g., lint dipped in the essence, compress placed on wound, duration held, bandage application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: lint wetted with the essence, held on the wound 'half a quarter of an hour'; compress and bandage described; in amputations the linen pledgets dipped in the astringent liquor with compress and bandage applied. Provide step-by-step application details so outcome can be judged or reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify time-to-effect and observable endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the time required for the remedy to produce its effect (e.g., blood stopped in four minutes, or in less than half a quarter of an hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account emphasizes rapidity of effect (calves' blood stopped in four minutes; human cases stopped quickly). Include measured times and observable criteria (no more blood, veins appear as if never opened).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report absence or presence of adverse effects and healing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess healing by noting absence of ill accident, suppuration, eschar, or visible cicatrix, and report patient comfort (pain relief, sleep).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors highlight that wounds healed 'without any visible cicatrice, and without any suppuration' and patients were 'free from pain' and slept. Use such clinical signs as key outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use severe and varied clinical scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the remedy in serious lesions (e.g., amputations, arterial wounds, fractured limbs from cannon-balls) as well as fluxes of blood and epistaxis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The liquor was tried on amputated limbs, axillary artery amputations, cannon-ball injuries, and nosebleeds; include a range of severities to demonstrate utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent verification by qualified witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Have surgeons, physicians, or other credible observers present to witness experiments and to report faithfully on results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The King sent physicians and surgeons to be present and 'faithfully to report' what passed; subsequent trials were conducted before the King and surgeons. Presence of reputable observers is used to persuade sceptics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication across species and contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Replicate experiments on different animals (dogs, calves) and in human patients and in different settings (hospitals, royal laboratory) to show robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments were repeated on dogs, calves, and human hospital patients; the King ordered quantities made and trials on calves at Whitehall. Cross-species replication and multiple contexts strengthen the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare effects to standard or expected outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare treated cases to usual healing expectations or to existing treatments (e.g., veins usually closed after 24 hours; contrast to cauterization with hot iron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors compare the rapid closure to the normal 24-hour closure of veins and note that patients escaped the pain of cauterization; comparisons to ordinary practice are used as evaluative benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide negative or null-result reporting and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report when an intended effect is not observed and note experimental limitations (e.g., inability to tinge the chyle under normal conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the chyle experiments they note consistent failure to discolor the lacteal chyle and conclude it 'not very feasible' without causing diabetes; honest reporting of negative findings and consideration of alternative means are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled variations of conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary experimental conditions systematically (e.g., feeding state: fed vs fasting; different dyes and vehicles) to test hypotheses about mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chyle experiments injected various tinged liquors, tried animals that were fed and fasting, and injected at different intestinal sites; such controlled variations are described as part of method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide morphological description and measurements in natural-history observations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting specimens (worms, anatomical features), give detailed morphology, counts, measurements, positions, and comparisons with known descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worms are described by length, thickness, colour, ring structure, position in gut, and compared to other authors and genera; such details enable identification and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diagrams, labeled parts, and precise dimensions for apparatus or constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: For devices or structures (bee-house, prosopographic parallelogram), supply figures with labeled parts and exact measurements and explain function of each part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bee-house section gives figure references, labels (A, B, C, etc.), and precise dimensions (e.g., 16 inches height, 23 breadth) and operational instructions (how to prevent swarming, how to harvest). The parallelogram description names parts and their roles. Visuals plus measurements are required for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain theoretical basis and practical application together
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting mathematical or mechanical work, divide exposition into clear parts: theory (lemmas, demonstrations) and mechanical construction or applications, with examples of successful use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slusius' method is presented via numbered lemmas leading 'by the hand' to the demonstration. Huygens' Horologium Oscillatorium is described as containing both geometry of curves and mechanical construction of watches, plus tables and voyage trials. Combine rigorous theory with practical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document provenance and sourcing of novel remedies or secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: When a remedy is secret or new, document how the secret was shared and who prepared or produced quantities, and note official endorsement or commissioning (e.g., King's laboratory produced doses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The King commanded M. Denis to communicate the secret and ordered production in his laboratory; documenting transmission and official production is included to establish reliability and availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report observational protocol and post-operative inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe follow-up inspection times and findings after treatment (e.g., dressings removed next morning; surgeons inspected wounds and judged them fair and ruddy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both human cases had dressings removed the next morning in presence of physicians who acknowledged good appearance. Include timing and who inspected wounds in follow-up.
